security.title: v1 ReportViewSet custom actions (edit_form/delete_form/share_form/flag) bypass object-level authz — edit/delete/re-share ANY report across ALL datasets by pk
security.description: ReportViewSet lists UserCreatedContentPermission in permission_classes, but DRF only runs has_object_permission when a view calls self.get_object(). All four custom @action methods fetch the object with `models.UserCreatedContent.objects.get(pk=pk)` (report.py:134,211,252,286) instead of self.get_object(), so has_object_permission is NEVER invoked and get_queryset()/get_viewable_reports() scoping is never applied. There is no dataset filter and no creator check. Concretely: `delete_form` POST calls oContent.delete() (report.py:288), `edit_form` POST saves arbitrary field/def changes (report.py:217-223), `share_form` POST rewrites sharing (report.py:260). Because the pk is a raw global primary key with no dataset/owner scoping, any user who reaches this viewset can target reports belonging to other users AND other datasets. authentication_classes=[CsrfExemptSessionAuthentication] also disables CSRF, so these destructive actions are additionally forgeable. The routes are live: chiron/api/urls.py:20 registers 'reports' and chiron/urls.py:101 includes 'api/'. The v2 equivalent (chiron/api_v2/viewsets/report.py:390,453,517) was explicitly fixed to use `get_object_or_404(self.get_queryset(), pk=pk)`, confirming this is the unfixed variant. Standard retrieve/update/destroy are NOT affected (they go through get_object).
security.impact: Horizontal + cross-tenant privilege escalation on a clinical-research tool. An authenticated user with subject-level (DEID/PHI) access to any one dataset can permanently delete, silently modify (including overwriting the cohort_def/table_def), or re-share any saved report in any dataset by iterating integer pks. share_form self-grant: an attacker in the same dataset as a victim can add their own ChironUser to a private (public=False) report's share list, causing it to appear in their get_viewable_reports and enabling full read/preview/export of the victim's private query and results. Data-integrity and confidentiality loss across dataset boundaries.
security.fix: Fetch through the scoped queryset and enforce object permissions in every custom action: replace `models.UserCreatedContent.objects.get(pk=pk)` with `oContent = self.get_object()` (which runs get_queryset()+check_object_permissions), or mirror v2 with `get_object_or_404(self.get_queryset(), pk=pk)`. For write actions (edit_form/delete_form/share_form) additionally require `oContent.creator == request.chironuser` (UserCreatedContentPermission already enforces creator-only for non-SAFE methods once get_object is used). Do not rely on public/shared visibility for write/delete. Remove CsrfExemptSessionAuthentication or add CSRF protection for state-changing endpoints.

verdict.reason: Verified all cited locations in chiron/api/viewsets/report.py. The four custom @action methods fetch objects with `models.UserCreatedContent.objects.get(pk=pk)` at lines 134 (flag), 211 (edit_form), 252 (share_form), 286 (delete_form) — a raw global primary-key lookup with no dataset or owner scoping. DRF only invokes check_object_permissions/has_object_permission when a view calls self.get_object(); these actions never do, so UserCreatedContentPermission.has_object_permission (permissions.py:40-52, the public/shared/creator owner check) is never run. The class-level has_permission (permissions.py:37-38) only checks is_authenticated. get_queryset()/get_viewable_reports() scoping — which filters by dataset via UserCreatedContent.objects.accessible(self.dataset) (user_models.py:130) plus creator/share/public — is therefore bypassed. delete_form line 288 calls oContent.delete() with no validation (fully cross-dataset); edit_form lines 217-223 save arbitrary field changes and can overwrite cohort_def/table_def with the attacker's active query via overwrite_query_def_with_active. The v2 equivalent (api_v2/viewsets/report.py lines 390, 453, 517) uses get_object_or_404(self.get_queryset(), pk=pk), confirming v1 is the unfixed variant. CsrfExemptSessionAuthentication (authentication.py) has an empty enforce_csrf, disabling CSRF on these state-changing POSTs (with an in-code TODO questioning the risk). Routes are live: api/urls.py:20 registers 'reports' and urls.py:101 includes 'api/'. The share_form self-grant is correctly bounded by the finding: ReportSharingForm scopes share_with to the creator's dataset (ui_forms.py:103-108) and clean() re-validates dataset match, so cross-dataset self-grant fails but same-dataset self-grant to a private report succeeds; delete/edit have no such barrier. Standard retrieve/update/destroy go through get_object and are unaffected, as claimed. Severity high (not critical): exploitation requires an authenticated user with PHI/DEID subject-level access to some dataset (SubjectLevelAccess gate, permissions.py:64-79), i.e. an authorized insider, but yields cross-tenant permanent deletion and silent modification of other users' saved reports.
verdict.corrected_fix: Replace `models.UserCreatedContent.objects.get(pk=pk)` in flag/edit_form/share_form/delete_form with `oContent = self.get_object()` (runs get_queryset() scoping + check_object_permissions) or mirror v2's `get_object_or_404(self.get_queryset(), pk=pk)`. Note that with get_object(), UserCreatedContentPermission.has_object_permission already enforces creator-only for non-SAFE methods (permissions.py:52), so an explicit creator check for edit/delete/share is satisfied — but the flag action is a POST too, so confirm whether flagging a public/shared report should be allowed (has_object_permission would restrict flag to the creator for POST, which may be unintended for starring; if starring of viewable reports is desired, gate flag on the SAFE-method read predicate instead). Also remove CsrfExemptSessionAuthentication or add CSRF enforcement for these state-changing endpoints.

security.title: Stored XSS: concept description rendered via dangerouslySetInnerHTML with no sanitization
security.location: is4r-chiron-ui-develop/src/routes/query.tsx:208-214 (sink at :211-212); data source is server field defined at is4r-chiron-develop/chiron/models/data_definition_models.py:646
security.description:
query.tsx renders the concept description as raw HTML: `
`. queryConceptData comes from the backend (store/cohortSlice.ts sets `queryConceptData: response` at ~line 572; description is typed at cohortSlice.ts:134) and maps to the Concept model's `description = models.TextField(...)` (data_definition_models.py:646), which is edited by staff through the Django admin (the in-app 'Edit Concept' button links to /admin/chiron/concept/, query.tsx:145-153). The TextField has no HTML sanitization on input, and dangerouslySetInnerHTML applies none on output. A description containing `` or `
security.impact: Stored/persistent XSS in a PHI-handling clinical tool. A user with concept-edit rights can plant a payload that runs in every viewer's authenticated session: because the API uses cookie auth with credentials:'include' (api/index.ts:9), the payload can issue authenticated API calls, exfiltrate PHI rendered on screen, and pivot across users — cross-user impact even if session cookies are httpOnly.
security.fix: Render the description through the same sanitizer used elsewhere: `<Interweave content={queryConceptData.description} />`, or sanitize with DOMPurify before injecting. Do not use dangerouslySetInnerHTML on server-authored HTML. Optionally sanitize/allowlist the description on the backend as defense-in-depth.

verdict.reason:
I independently opened every cited location and confirmed the vulnerability end-to-end.

SINK: query.tsx lines 208-214 render `queryConceptData.description` via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: queryConceptData.description }}` with no sanitization. This is the ONLY dangerouslySetInnerHTML in src/ (grep confirmed) — every other server-HTML render uses <Interweave> (DescribeFilters.tsx:65, CriteriaSet.tsx:150/219/298), which sanitizes. interweave version confirmed as 13.1.1. So the finding's "inconsistent oversight" framing is accurate.

DATA FLOW: cohortSlice.ts:572 sets `queryConceptData: response` directly from the API thunk response; ConceptData.description is typed `string` at cohortSlice.ts:134. Backend serializer ConceptSerializer (api_v2/serializers/concept.py:25-65) exposes `description` as a plain ModelSerializer field (line 49) with no sanitizing SerializerMethodField — raw model value passes straight through. The underlying field is `Concept.description = models.TextField(blank=True, null=True)` (data_definition_models.py:886), edited by staff via the Django admin (Edit Concept link, query.tsx:145-153, gated by isStaff). No input-side sanitization exists: the only strip_tags on concept.description is in the ETL export path (chiron_etl.py:214), not the API path. api/index.ts:9 confirms `credentials: "include"` cookie auth, so a planted payload runs with the victim's authenticated session.

CITATION CORRECTION: the finding cites data_definition_models.py:646 as the Concept description field, but line 646 is actually PermissionGroup.description. The real Concept.description is line 886. This is a wrong line number only; the substance (a Concept TextField serialized raw and rendered via dangerouslySetInnerHTML) is fully correct.

SEVERITY: Genuine stored XSS in a PHI-handling clinical tool with cross-user execution (a payload planted by a concept-editor runs in every viewer's authenticated session, enabling PHI exfiltration and authenticated API calls). The one mitigating factor is that write access requires an authenticated staff user with concept-edit rights (Django admin), so it is a privileged-write / privilege-escalation vector rather than unauthenticated input. Given the cross-user impact and PHI exposure, high is appropriate.
verdict.corrected_fix: Render via the same sanitizer used elsewhere: `<Interweave content={queryConceptData.description} />` (matching DescribeFilters.tsx / CriteriaSet.tsx). If raw block-level HTML must be preserved, sanitize with DOMPurify before injection. As defense-in-depth, sanitize/allowlist the description server-side in ConceptSerializer or on model save, since input arrives via Django admin and django_autocreate (field.help_text at django_autocreate.py:306) with no escaping.

security.title: ETL log / data-issue views expose raw subject-matching identifiers and source values with no dataset scoping and no access-level check (cross-dataset IDOR + PHI-tier bypass)
security.location: is4r-chiron-develop/chiron/views/views_backend.py:79-173 (etl_logs:100, etl_log_details:112, source_data_issues:122, source_record_subject_matching:135, record_logs_for_subject:157-160); templates chiron/templates/chiron/backend/source_record_subject_matching.html:74-88, record_logs_for_subject.html:55-68, source_data_issues.html:47-63; data written in chiron/etl/logger.py:131-139,151-158
security.description: All five ETL-log views are gated only by @login_required + @dataset_selector + @user_passes_test(user_is_staff). user_is_staff (chiron/authorization.py:13-19) checks Django's GLOBAL request.user.is_staff, and dataset_selector only requires that the user has *some* ChironUser on the active dataset -- it never inspects request.chironuser.access_level. The queries are also never scoped to request.dataset: etl_logs runs models.EtlLog.objects.all() (views_backend.py:100), and the detail views do get_object_or_404(EtlLog/SourceEtlLog, pk=<url value>) (lines 112, 122, 135, 157) with the numeric id / subject_id taken straight from the URL and no dataset filter, even though EtlLog carries a dataset field (log_models.py:15). The rendered rows contain the most sensitive raw linkage data: SourceRecordEtlLog.subject_id / add_ids / subject_final_ids / match_def (log_models.py:118-128, populated verbatim in logger.py:151-158 from the actual subject-match identifiers -- MRN/name/DOB-type values) and ConceptIssueExampleEtlLog.input_value / stored_value (log_models.py:154-157, populated in logger.py:131-139 with literal source-record values that triggered a data issue). Two distinct authz failures result: (1) Cross-dataset IDOR -- a staff user of dataset A can enumerate/guess ids and read dataset B's raw subject-matching data and example values (e.g. /backend/etl_logs/<id>/source/<source_log_id>, /backend/etl_logs/<log_id>/subject/<subject_id>), and etl_logs lists every dataset's runs; (2) Access-tier bypass -- a DEID- or AGG-level staff ChironUser, who is by design forbidden from viewing PHI/subject-level identifiers, sees them here because access_level is never checked. This directly contradicts the per-dataset, per-tier model enforced elsewhere (e.g. data_definition_models.py:1101-1103 blocks cross-dataset concept access; 1108-1132 gates PHI by access_level).
security.impact: An authenticated staff user with access to any single dataset can read raw patient-identifying match keys (subject ids, added ids, match rules) and literal source data example values for ALL datasets in the instance, and can do so even when their own access tier is DEID or AGG. This breaks both multi-tenant isolation and the PHI/DEID/AGG access model for the most sensitive (re-identifying) data the system stores.
security.fix: 1) Scope every query to the active dataset: models.EtlLog.objects.filter(dataset=request.dataset.unique_id); for detail views use get_object_or_404(EtlLog, pk=log_id, dataset=request.dataset.unique_id) and chain the child lookups (e.g. get_object_or_404(SourceEtlLog, pk=source_log_id, etl_log__dataset=request.dataset.unique_id); SourceRecordEtlLog.objects.filter(source_log__etl_log__dataset=request.dataset.unique_id, ...)). 2) Replace/augment the is_staff-only gate with a per-dataset PHI check, e.g. require request.chironuser.access_level == ChironUser.AccessLevel.PHI (subject-matching logs contain identifiers), or an explicit 'can view ETL logs' permission -- global is_staff is insufficient. 3) Consider not persisting raw identifier/example values (or masking them) in SourceRecordEtlLog/ConceptIssueExampleEtlLog since they duplicate PHI outside the tiered query engine.

verdict.reason: Verified all cited locations. views_backend.py: the five ETL-log views (etl_logs L100, etl_log_details L112, source_data_issues L122, source_record_subject_matching L135, record_logs_for_subject L157-160) are gated only by @login_required + @dataset_selector + @user_passes_test(user_is_staff). authorization.py:13-19 confirms user_is_staff returns Django's GLOBAL user.is_staff; dataset_selector (76-102) only ensures a ChironUser exists for the active dataset and never checks access_level. None of the queries filter by dataset: etl_logs uses EtlLog.objects.all() (lists every dataset's runs, paginated), and the detail views call get_object_or_404 on the raw URL pk/subject_id with no dataset constraint, despite EtlLog carrying a dataset field (log_models.py:15). urls.py:36-51 exposes all views with attacker-controlled integer/string path params, confirming the IDOR surface. The rendered rows contain raw re-identifying linkage data: SourceRecordEtlLog.match_def/add_ids/subject_id/subject_final_ids (log_models.py:118-128) written verbatim from subject_match_manager in logger.py:151-158, and ConceptIssueExampleEtlLog.input_value/stored_value (log_models.py:154-157) written from literal source values in logger.py:131-139; the three cited templates render these fields directly. This bypasses the model enforced elsewhere: data_definition_models.py:1101-1103 blocks cross-dataset concept access and 1108-1132 gates PHI by access_level, with AccessLevel PHI/DEID/AGG defined in user_models.py:51-54 and ChironUser defaulting to DEID (L95). Both failures are real: (1) cross-dataset IDOR — a staff user of one dataset can enumerate ids to read any dataset's subject-matching identifiers and example values; (2) tier bypass — a DEID/AGG staff ChironUser sees subject-level identifiers because access_level is never checked. Severity high is correct: it requires an authenticated staff account (not pre-auth, so not critical) but exposes re-identifying PHI across tenants in a hospital system. One refinement: the concept-issue example values (source_data_issues) are persisted during normal finalize_source_log on every ETL run, not only under --track-subject-matching, so that leak is not conditional on the flag.
verdict.corrected_fix: Apply the proposed dataset scoping and tier check, which are accurate: 1) etl_logs -> EtlLog.objects.filter(dataset=request.dataset.unique_id) (EtlLog.dataset stores the slug unique_id per logger.py:34, so match on request.dataset.unique_id, not the Dataset object). 2) Detail views: etl_log_details -> get_object_or_404(EtlLog, pk=log_id, dataset=request.dataset.unique_id); source_data_issues/source_record_subject_matching -> get_object_or_404(SourceEtlLog, pk=source_log_id, etl_log__dataset=request.dataset.unique_id); record_logs_for_subject -> scope the EtlLog lookup and the SourceRecordEtlLog filter with source_log__etl_log__dataset=request.dataset.unique_id. 3) Add a per-dataset PHI gate for the subject-matching views (and ideally source_data_issues, since example values are literal source data): require request.chironuser.access_level == ChironUser.AccessLevel.PHI (or a dedicated 'can view ETL logs' permission), because global is_staff does not enforce the tier model. 4) Longer term, consider masking or not persisting raw identifier/example values in SourceRecordEtlLog/ConceptIssueExampleEtlLog so PHI does not live outside the tiered query engine.

security.title: v1 report_tools load_as_active/export_csv/export_json/preview: no ownership/sharing/dataset scoping (IDOR on saved reports)
security.description: Each of these actions does `get_object_or_404(models.UserCreatedContent, pk=pk)` with no dataset, creator, share, or public check, then reads the report's cohort_def/table_def via oContent.get_def_value(...) and either loads them into the caller's active snapshot (load_as_active), or executes them (export/preview). ReportToolsViewSet.permission_classes is [IsAuthenticated, DatasetSelector, SubjectLevelAccess] with no object-level permission class, and the actions never call get_object(). By contrast, the sibling `share` action (report_tools.py:68) DOES gate on `user_content.creator != request.chironuser` and is therefore safe for writes; only these four read/execute actions are unprotected. The v2 version (chiron/api_v2/viewsets/report_tools.py:113,141,165,212) added `.filter(dataset=request.dataset)`, confirming v1 is the unfixed variant. Note the query itself is executed as request.chironuser via export_utils.generate_cohort_csv/json / get_paginated_preview (chiron/api/utils/export.py:14,68,146), so returned rows are limited to the caller's own access scope — the leak is the victim's saved query DEFINITION and unauthorized execution, not direct PHI over-disclosure.
security.impact: Any authenticated user with subject-level access can enumerate report pks (global integers) across all datasets and disclose other researchers' private cohort/table definitions (which encode sensitive research criteria, e.g. diagnosis/age/medication inclusion filters) via load_as_active/preview, and run arbitrary saved reports. Confidentiality of research intent and saved-query IP across users and datasets.
security.fix: Scope the lookup to reports the caller may view, e.g. `get_object_or_404(request.chironuser.get_viewable_reports(), pk=pk)`, or at minimum `.filter(dataset=request.dataset)` as v2 does (note v2 still leaves same-dataset private reports exposed — prefer get_viewable_reports() to also enforce creator/shared/public). Apply consistently to load_as_active, export_csv, export_json, and preview.

verdict.reason: Verified all four cited actions in chiron/api/viewsets/report_tools.py: load_as_active (:114), export_csv (:140), export_json (:162), preview (:207) each do get_object_or_404(models.UserCreatedContent, pk=pk) with zero dataset/creator/share/public scoping, then read cohort_def/table_def and load/execute them. permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated, DatasetSelector, SubjectLevelAccess]; reading permissions.py, DatasetSelector only sets request.dataset/chironuser and SubjectLevelAccess only checks PHI/DEID level — neither is object-level. The correct object-level class UserCreatedContentPermission (with has_object_permission checking public/share_with/creator) exists in the same file but is NOT in this viewset's list, and the actions never call get_object(), so DRF runs no object check. The share action (:68-73) genuinely gates on creator != request.chironuser, confirming only these four read/execute paths are unprotected. api_v2/viewsets/report_tools.py adds .filter(dataset=request.dataset) to all four (:113,:141,:165,:212), confirming v1 is the unfixed variant. export.py confirms queries run as request.chironuser (generate_cohort_csv/json get_paginated_preview all pass chironuser=request.chironuser), so returned rows respect the caller's own access scope — the leak is the victim's saved query DEFINITION plus unauthorized execution, exactly as claimed, not direct PHI over-disclosure. ChironUser.get_viewable_reports() exists (user_models.py:129) and scopes to dataset + Q(creator|share_with|public), so the proposed fix is real and correct. Cross-user private (public=False) and cross-dataset reports are demonstrably exposed. Medium is appropriate: confidentiality of research intent/saved-query IP and unauthorized query execution, no direct PHI leak.
verdict.corrected_fix: In each of load_as_active, export_csv, export_json, and preview in chiron/api/viewsets/report_tools.py, replace get_object_or_404(models.UserCreatedContent, pk=pk) with get_object_or_404(request.chironuser.get_viewable_reports(), pk=pk). This enforces dataset scoping plus creator/shared/public access in one call, matching the existing object-level policy in UserCreatedContentPermission and improving on v2's dataset-only filter (which still leaves same-dataset private reports exposed).

security.title: Snapshot retrieve IDOR: cohort_def/table_def/analysis_def read any user's saved definition by pk (v1 all three; v2 cohort_def also)
security.location: chiron/api/viewsets/cohort_def.py:90; chiron/api/viewsets/table_def.py:83; chiron/api/viewsets/analysis_def.py:91; chiron/api_v2/viewsets/cohort_def.py:9-25 (inherits vulnerable retrieve)
security.description: The retrieve methods call `get_object_or_404(models.CohortDefSnapshot|TableDefSnapshot|AnalysisDefSnapshot, pk=pk)` with no filter on the owning chironuser. These snapshot models are strictly per-user (chironuser FK: chiron/models/user_models.py:179,290,404) and per-dataset by extension. The response returns get_cohort_def()/get_table_def()/get_analysis_def() plus previous_snapshot_id/next_snapshot_id (which are computed against the victim's own chironuser, chiron/models/user_models.py:246-262/357-377, leaking adjacent snapshot pks). set_active is safe (it re-filters by chironuser), but the definition is still returned. v2 explicitly fixed table_def (chiron/api_v2/viewsets/table_def.py:41) and analysis_def (chiron/api_v2/viewsets/analysis_def.py:37) with `.filter(chironuser=request.chironuser)`, but v2 cohort_def (chiron/api_v2/viewsets/cohort_def.py) only overrides get_queryset and INHERITS the vulnerable v1 retrieve — and that retrieve hard-codes the unscoped lookup and never consults get_queryset, so the v2 get_queryset override is dead code and v2 cohort_def retrieve remains vulnerable.
security.impact: Any authenticated user with workspace/subject-level access can read any other user's in-progress cohort, table, or analysis definitions (and walk their snapshot history) by iterating integer pks, cross-user and cross-dataset. Cohort definitions are the most sensitive (encode subject selection criteria). Confidentiality of unsaved research work.
security.fix: Scope every retrieve to the owner: `get_object_or_404(models.CohortDefSnapshot.objects.filter(chironuser=request.chironuser), pk=pk)` (and the analogous change for table_def/analysis_def v1). For v2 cohort_def, add a retrieve override that uses the scoped queryset (as v2 table_def/analysis_def already do), since the inherited retrieve ignores get_queryset().

verdict.reason: Verified all cited locations. v1 retrieve methods use unscoped get_object_or_404: cohort_def.py:90 (CohortDefSnapshot), table_def.py:83 (TableDefSnapshot), analysis_def.py:91 (AnalysisDefSnapshot), each fetching a snapshot by pk with no chironuser filter, then returning get_cohort_def()/get_table_def()/clean_analysis_def() plus previous/next snapshot ids. Confirmed the snapshot models are strictly per-user via a chironuser FK (user_models.py:179, 290, 404), and get_previous()/get_next() (lines 246-262) filter by self.chironuser (the fetched/victim snapshot's owner), so previous_snapshot_id/next_snapshot_id leak the victim's adjacent snapshot pks. set_active is guarded (model set_active re-filters by chironuser, lines 224-234) but the definition body is returned regardless. Confirmed v2 table_def.py:41-43 and analysis_def.py:37-39 fixed this with objects.filter(chironuser=request.chironuser). Confirmed v2 cohort_def.py only overrides get_queryset (lines 21-25); its base is viewsets.ViewSet (v1 cohort_def.py:20), not a GenericViewSet, and the inherited v1 retrieve hard-codes the unscoped lookup and never calls get_queryset(), so the override is dead code and v2 cohort_def retrieve remains vulnerable. retrieve uses get_object_or_404 directly (not self.get_object()), so no object-level permission check runs; the listed permission_classes only gate general dataset/workspace access, not snapshot ownership. Genuine cross-user IDOR reachable by iterating integer pks. Medium severity is appropriate: authenticated-only, exposes in-progress definition metadata (subject-selection criteria), not raw patient data.
verdict.corrected_fix: Scope each v1 retrieve to the owner: oSnapshot = get_object_or_404(models.CohortDefSnapshot.objects.filter(chironuser=request.chironuser), pk=pk) (and analogous TableDefSnapshot/AnalysisDefSnapshot changes). For v2 cohort_def, add a retrieve override that uses the scoped queryset, matching v2 table_def/analysis_def, since the inherited ViewSet.retrieve ignores get_queryset(). Optionally refactor to self.get_object() with a shared get_queryset so object-level scoping is centralized.

security.title: ChironUserViewSet returns all users across ALL datasets — cross-dataset PII enumeration
security.description: get_queryset returns `models.ChironUser.objects.order_by('user__last_name')` with no filter on request.dataset. permission_classes is only [IsAuthenticated, DatasetSelector] (no workspace/subject-level gate). ChironUserSerializer exposes each user's first_name, last_name, email (via nested UserSerializer, serializers.py:24-27), access_level, and permission_groups. The `term` query param (chiron_user.py:22-27) allows searching by email/name, enabling targeted lookup. ChironUser is explicitly a per-dataset object (user_models.py:86-113, unique_together dataset+user), and the intended scoping exists elsewhere in the codebase (v2 report.py:254 filters share candidates by `dataset=oContent.creator.dataset`), so the missing dataset filter here is a defect, not by design.
security.impact: In any multi-dataset deployment, an authenticated user with access to a single dataset can enumerate the full roster of researchers/staff across every dataset, including names, email addresses, access levels, and permission-group membership. PII disclosure and reconnaissance for targeting other datasets' users.
security.fix: Filter to the active dataset: `models.ChironUser.objects.filter(dataset=self.request.dataset).order_by('user__last_name')` (request.dataset is set by DatasetSelector). Consider restricting the endpoint to users who need the share picker and trimming email exposure.

verdict.reason: All claims verified against source. chiron/api/viewsets/chiron_user.py:19 returns `models.ChironUser.objects.order_by("user__last_name")` with no dataset filter; it's a ReadOnlyModelViewSet registered at `chiron_users` (chiron/api/urls.py:7) protected only by [IsAuthenticated, DatasetSelector]. ChironUserSerializer (serializers.py:30-50) exposes nested user first_name/last_name/email/username (UserSerializer, lines 24-27) plus access_level and permission_groups. The `term` param (chiron_user.py:22-27) enables icontains search by name/email across all datasets. ChironUser is per-dataset (user_models.py:86,112-113: dataset FK, unique_together dataset+user). Multi-dataset is a supported mode (authorization.py:38-41; DatasetSelector error text references "multiple datasets"). The intended scoping exists elsewhere: api_v2/viewsets/report.py:254 filters share candidates by `dataset=oContent.creator.dataset` with an explicit comment, confirming the omission here is a defect not design. request.dataset is set by DatasetSelector (permissions.py:27), so the proposed fix is applicable. Impact is bounded to staff/researcher PII (not patient PHI) and only manifests in multi-dataset deployments, so medium (not high) is correct.
verdict.corrected_fix: In get_queryset, scope to the active dataset before other filters: `queryset = models.ChironUser.objects.filter(dataset=self.request.dataset).order_by("user__last_name")`. request.dataset is guaranteed set by DatasetSelector.has_permission. security.title: view_as_other_user impersonation has no target restrictions or audit; enables staff→superuser escalation
security.description: The ViewAsOtherUser middleware reads session['override_user_id'] and unconditionally sets request.user to that Django user for the whole request (and thus for downstream DRF permission checks). The middleware performs no authorization itself. The only writer of override_user_id is the user_report view (views_backend.py:216-219), which is correctly gated by @user_passes_test(user_is_staff) — so arbitrary users cannot start impersonation. However, once gated, `override_user_id = int(request.POST.get('override_user_id'))` accepts ANY user id with no constraint: no check that the target belongs to the current dataset, no check that the target is not a superuser or higher-privileged, and no audit record. Because the middleware replaces request.user globally, an impersonated identity also applies to Django admin (which authorizes on request.user.is_staff/is_superuser). The middleware is a shippable, opt-in component and is installed in the reference settings (test_project/project/settings.py:62). Also `int(request.POST.get('override_user_id', None))` raises TypeError (500) when the field is absent — robustness bug.
security.impact: A Chiron 'staff' user (which is distinct from a Django superuser in this app and gates only Chiron admin views) can impersonate a Django superuser via override_user_id and then act as that superuser everywhere, including /admin/ — a staff→superuser privilege escalation. More generally, impersonation of any user in any dataset with no logging undermines attribution and the dataset access boundary.
security.fix: In the setter, validate the target: reject users with is_superuser (or any privilege ≥ the impersonator), require the target to have a ChironUser in the current dataset, and write an audit log entry (impersonator, target, timestamp). Guard the int() parse against missing/non-numeric input. Optionally have the middleware re-verify that the impersonation was established by a still-staff session and scope its effect away from the Django admin.

security.title: CSRF protection disabled on session-authenticated, state-changing API endpoints (shipped library)

security.title: Hardcoded Django SECRET_KEY in reference project — also used as the de-identification salt for subject IDs

security.description: SECRET_KEY is a hardcoded literal ('1b_762p=...') in the runnable reference/demo settings. Beyond the usual session-cookie / password-reset-token signing exposure, the shipped ETL processors EtlGeneratedSubjectId/EtlGeneratedSubcollectionId use settings.SECRET_KEY directly as the salt for the blake2b hash that generates de-identified subject and sub-collection IDs (auto_subject_id.py:60, :71 and :120, :131). The default output length of 10 yields only a 5-byte/40-bit digest, further easing brute-force re-identification.
security.impact: Copied/leaked key enables session forgery and, more importantly for a clinical tool, defeats subject de-identification (re-identification of patient-like records).
security.fix: Load SECRET_KEY from an environment variable / secret store and fail closed if unset; keep only a clearly-labeled throwaway value in the demo. Additionally, decouple the de-identification salt from SECRET_KEY (use a dedicated, per-deployment secret consumed via blake2b's key= parameter) and increase the default digest length.

security.title: Missing and misspelled HTTP security headers (broken HSTS, no CSP/X-Frame-Options/nosniff)
security.description: nginx.conf:28 sets `add_header Strict-Transprot-Securty max-age=2592000;` — the header name is misspelled ('Strict-Transprot-Securty' instead of 'Strict-Transport-Security'), so browsers receive an unknown header and no HSTS is enforced; the value also lacks includeSubDomains. Line 28 is verbatim `add_header Strict-Transprot-Securty max-age=2592000;` — the header name is misspelled twice ('Transprot' should be 'Transport', 'Securty' should be 'Security'), so browsers receive an unrecognized custom header and no HSTS is applied; the value also omits includeSubDomains. security.description: The ETL/DDL code builds SQL by directly interpolating metadata identifiers into raw text() strings, not via bound parameters or a proper identifier quoter. Examples: db_writer.py:78 `sql = f'TRUNCATE TABLE "{schema_name}".{collection.permanent_id} RESTART IDENTITY'` then `conn.execute(text(sql))` (collection.permanent_id is completely UNQUOTED); db_writer.py:88/91 `f'DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS "{schema_name}" CASCADE'` / `f'CREATE SCHEMA "{schema_name}"'`; db_writer.py:144/153/156 `ALTER/DROP SCHEMA "{...}"`; db_writer.py:385 `f'DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "{schema_name}".concept_search'`; db_writer.py:449-452/463-466 `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS {index_name} ON "{schema_name}"."{table_name}" ("{oConcept.permanent_id}")` (index_name is UNQUOTED, and the column/table names rely only on a single pair of double quotes with no escaping of embedded quotes). database.py:54 `options_str = "-csearch_path={}".format(schema_name)` injects the schema into the libpq connection options string (an embedded space would let an attacker append arbitrary `-c` server options). These identifiers derive from Django SlugField columns (data_definition_models.py:57 database_name, :371/:879 permanent_id, :53 unique_id) whose charset [-a-zA-Z0-9_] would, IF ENFORCED, make injection impossible. But Django SlugField validators only run on full_clean()/ModelForm.is_valid(); a repo-wide grep shows full_clean is never called (only a commented-out clean_fields at data_definition_models.py:445), and SlugField creates a plain varchar with no DB CHECK constraint. The programmatic creation paths bypass validation entirely: csv_autocreate.py:249-250 sets `oConcept.permanent_id = '{}_{}'.format(field_name, random_string())` where field_name is a raw CSV column header, then csv_autocreate.py:299 calls `.save()` directly (no full_clean); csv_autocreate.py:62-66 creates a Dataset with `database_name=dataset_name` from ETL settings; csv_autocreate.py:96-99 sets Collection.permanent_id from settings. Data flow to sink: crafted CSV column header (e.g. `evt") ; DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE; --`) -> Concept.permanent_id -> db_writer.create_indexes() f-string DDL -> text()/execute during ETL. Because these are DDL statements run by a DB role that owns every dataset schema, successful injection can drop or alter arbitrary schemas (including other datasets') or run arbitrary SQL.
security.impact: An actor able to influence source data loaded during ETL (crafted CSV headers) or ETL config values (database_name / collection ids) can inject arbitrary DDL/SQL that executes with the warehouse-owner role, enabling destruction or tampering of any dataset schema in the Postgres warehouse. This is an ETL/data-curation trust-boundary issue, not reachable by an ordinary authenticated API user, which is why it is Medium rather than Critical. The SlugField gives a false sense of safety because its validation is never actually enforced on the paths that ingest external strings.
security.fix: Do not interpolate identifiers into SQL text. For DDL, quote every identifier with a real quoter (SQLAlchemy `engine.dialect.identifier_preparer.quote(name)` / `quote_schema`, or psycopg2 `psycopg.sql.Identifier`), and never leave any identifier unquoted (index_name at db_writer.py:449 and collection.permanent_id at :78 are unquoted). Independently, enforce the slug constraint at the trust boundary: call `full_clean()` (or explicitly `django.core.validators.validate_slug`) in csv_autocreate.py/django_autocreate.py before saving Dataset/Collection/Concept, and add a strict `re.fullmatch(r'[A-Za-z0-9_]+', name)` allowlist check on schema/table/column names in database.py/db_writer.py before they reach any SQL string. For database.py:54, validate that schema_name matches the slug allowlist so no whitespace can smuggle extra libpq `-c` options.

verdict.reason: Every cited location was opened and matches the claim. chiron/query_engine/postgres/db_writer.py builds DDL by raw f-string interpolation of metadata identifiers and runs it via conn.execute(text(sql)): line 78 TRUNCATE with collection.permanent_id UNQUOTED; lines 88/91/144/153/156 DROP/CREATE/ALTER SCHEMA "{...}"; line 385 DROP TABLE; and lines 449-452/463-466 CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS {index_name} where index_name = f"idx_{oConcept.permanent_id}" (line 438) is COMPLETELY UNQUOTED and the column reference ("{oConcept.permanent_id}") uses one pair of double quotes with no escaping of embedded quotes. database.py:54 does options_str = "-csearch_path={}".format(schema_name), later passed as the libpq options connect arg (line 71), so whitespace could smuggle extra -c server options. The taint is real: csv_autocreate.py:169-188 reads field_names straight from CSV column headers (record.keys()) with no sanitization; get_concepts (250) sets oConcept.permanent_id = "{}_{}".format(field_name, random_string()); save_concepts (299) calls concept.save() with no full_clean(). A repo-wide grep confirms full_clean/validate_slug are never called in chiron source (only a commented-out clean_fields at data_definition_models.py:445 that concerns event-field consistency, not slug charset). database_name/permanent_id/unique_id are all SlugField (lines 53,57,371,879), whose validate_slug runs only during full_clean/form validation, never on Model.save(); the sole save() override (Source, 257) merely calls super(). create_indexes() is reached during ETL (chiron_etl.py:112). Thus a crafted CSV header flows unsanitized into unquoted DDL executed by the warehouse-owner role; the unquoted index_name enables multi-statement injection (psycopg2 allows ;-separated statements when no params are bound), with a trailing -- commenting out the appended random suffix. Medium is the correct severity: this is an operator-facing ETL/data-curation trust boundary, not reachable by an ordinary authenticated API user, but successful injection can drop/alter arbitrary schemas. The proposed fix (quote every identifier with a real quoter such as dialect.identifier_preparer.quote/quote_schema or psycopg.sql.Identifier, never leave index_name/collection.permanent_id unquoted, plus enforce a strict slug allowlist / full_clean at the ingest boundary and validate schema_name before the libpq options string) is specific and appropriate.
verdict.corrected_fix: Adopt the proposed fix. Priorities: (1) In db_writer.create_indexes, stop interpolating raw identifiers — quote index_name, table_name, schema_name and the column name with engine.dialect.identifier_preparer.quote()/quote_schema() (or build the DDL with psycopg.sql.Identifier); index_name at line 449/463 and collection.permanent_id at line 78 are currently fully unquoted and are the primary injection sinks. (2) Enforce the slug constraint at the trust boundary: in csv_autocreate.py before .save(), run full_clean() or django.core.validators.validate_slug on Concept/Collection/Dataset, or apply re.fullmatch(r'[A-Za-z0-9_]+', name) to field-derived identifiers before they become permanent_id. (3) In database.py:54 validate schema_name against the slug allowlist so no whitespace can inject additional libpq -c options. Defense in depth: since these are DDL that cannot use bound parameters, the identifier quoter plus an allowlist is the correct combination.

security.title: Concept retrieve returns concept metadata without dataset check (low-sensitivity cross-dataset leak)
security.description: retrieve/update fetch `get_object_or_404(models.Concept, permanent_id=permanent_id)` and return serializer.data directly, bypassing get_queryset() (concept.py:55-112) which filters by published and per-user user_can_view_concept_stats(). Concept.permanent_id is globally unique (data_definition_models.py:879) and concepts are dataset-scoped only via collection.dataset (data_definition_models.py:896), so a user in one dataset can read another dataset's concept metadata (name, description, has_phi flag, options) by permanent_id (a guessable slug). The sensitive path — statistics/cohort options — is separately re-gated by user_can_view_concept_stats(), which DOES enforce the dataset boundary (data_definition_models.py:1101) and permission groups, so aggregate/statistical data is NOT leaked; only static schema metadata is.
security.impact: Minor schema/field-description disclosure across datasets. No patient data or statistics exposed because the statistics/options code paths re-check user_can_view_concept_stats().
security.fix: Fetch concept metadata through the dataset-scoped queryset, e.g. `get_object_or_404(models.Concept.objects.filter(collection__dataset=request.dataset), permanent_id=permanent_id)`, in retrieve and update.

verdict.reason: Verified all cited locations. concept.py:157 (retrieve) and :190 (update) call get_object_or_404(models.Concept, permanent_id=permanent_id) directly on the unfiltered manager and return serializer.data — they neither route through get_queryset() (concept.py:55-112, which filters published + user_can_view_concept_stats) nor call self.get_object(), so DRF's check_object_permissions is also never invoked. permanent_id is a globally unique SlugField (data_definition_models.py:879), and dataset scoping exists only via collection.dataset (concept FK at :896; ConceptManager.accessible at :869 filters collection__dataset). user_can_view_concept_stats (:1089) explicitly enforces the boundary at :1101 (chironuser.dataset != self.collection.dataset), confirming a dataset boundary is intended. The permission classes (DatasetSelector, SubjectLevelAccess in permissions.py:8-79) only implement view-level has_permission and set request.dataset/chironuser from the session's active dataset independent of the fetched concept — no object-level dataset gate. ConceptSerializer (api/serializers.py:83-122) exposes name, description, has_phi, collection names, category_hierarchy, prefilter_mode, concept_for_prefilter, etc. Net effect: a user authenticated to dataset A can retrieve dataset B's concept schema metadata by guessing/knowing its slug. I also confirmed the finding's mitigating claim: the statistics path (_get_concept_statistics :219-221) and the cohort/table option paths (via get_cohort_def_processor :1231 / get_display_processor :1248 -> user_can_use_concept_in_cohort_def -> user_can_view_concept_stats) are independently re-gated and return errors/empty results cross-dataset, so no statistics/patient data leak — only static metadata. This is a genuine but low-severity cross-tenant metadata disclosure, exploitable only in multi-dataset deployments by an authenticated user. Severity low is correctly scoped and not over-claimed.
verdict.corrected_fix: Scope the lookup to the active dataset in both retrieve and update: article = get_object_or_404(models.Concept.objects.filter(collection__dataset=request.dataset), permanent_id=permanent_id). The proposed fix is valid since request.dataset is populated by DatasetSelector. A stronger, more consistent alternative is to fetch via self.get_queryset() (article = get_object_or_404(self.get_queryset(), permanent_id=permanent_id)), which additionally applies the published + user_can_view_concept_stats filtering already used by list(), yielding a 404 for any concept the user cannot view rather than only enforcing the dataset boundary.

security.title: Reference/demo Django settings omit all session, CSRF, and transport security flags
security.location: test_project/project/settings.py (no SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE / CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE / SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT / SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS anywhere; grep across test_project/ and chiron/ returns none)
security.description: The settings define no cookie- or transport-hardening at all, so all of SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE, CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE, SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT, and SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS fall back to their insecure Django defaults (False / 0). Session and CSRF cookies will therefore be transmitted over plain HTTP. This is the reference project consumers start from; combined with DEBUG=True (settings.py:29), a deployment based on it would leak cookies and tracebacks. (SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY defaults to True, which is fine.)
security.impact: Session/CSRF cookies sent over HTTP are interceptable on the network; for patient-like data this enables session hijacking. Demo/reference config, but the pattern propagates to real deployments.
security.fix: In the reference settings (or a documented production settings module) set SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True, CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE=True, SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT=True, SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS>0 with includeSubDomains, and gate them behind an env flag so dev stays usable. Ship these as the secure default and let developers opt out locally.

verdict.reason: Verified is4r-chiron-develop/test_project/project/settings.py (cited path; not in benchmark cwd but in the sibling chiron repo). The file genuinely contains no SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE / CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE / SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT / SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS — grep across test_project/ and chiron/ returned zero matches — and DEBUG=True is on line 29 as claimed. SessionMiddleware (l.56) and CsrfViewMiddleware (l.58) are enabled, so those flags fall back to Django's insecure defaults. So the technical condition described is factually accurate. However, the severity is over-claimed: this is explicitly a dev/test harness, not a production reference template. The docstring calls it 'chiron_demo project'; lines 22-28 carry Django's standard 'unsuitable for production' and DEBUG/secret-key SECURITY WARNINGs; it ships a hardcoded SECRET_KEY (l.26), SQLite, empty ALLOWED_HOSTS, sys.path.append('..') 'attach to local version of chiron', and an infobar 'small dummy database for testing'. Missing cookie-secure flags in such a file are just Django startproject defaults; forcing SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT=True here would break local HTTP dev, and there is no production deployment or real patient data. The 'reference project consumers start from' and 'patient data session hijacking' framing is speculative. Real as a hardening note, but low/informational rather than medium.
verdict.corrected_fix: Leave the test project as dev-only (it is self-labeled unsuitable for production). Put the hardening in a production settings module instead: the file already provides the override hook `from .settings_custom import *` (l.156-159) and a separate performance_project settings exists. In that production module set SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True, CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE=True, SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT=True, and SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS>0 with SECURE_HSTS_INCLUDE_SUBDOMAINS=True, and document running `manage.py check --deploy`. Do not hardcode these True in the shared dev settings, which would break local HTTP work.

security.title: Vite dev server sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * (dev-only)
security.description: server.headers sets 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': '*' on the Vite dev server. This applies only to the local dev server (port 3000) and is not emitted by the production build served through nginx, so it does not affect deployed instances. While a developer is running the dev server, any origin the developer browses to could read responses proxied through it (which forwards /api, /admin, /accounts to the Django backend at 127.0.0.1:8000).
security.impact: Limited to developer machines running the dev server; a malicious site visited during development could read proxied backend responses cross-origin.
security.fix: Remove the wildcard CORS header; Vite does not need it for the SPA-to-proxy flow. If a specific cross-origin dev scenario requires it, scope it to explicit localhost origins.

verdict.reason: At /Users/pot95a/2026/new_chiron/is4r-chiron-ui-develop/vite.config.ts lines 9-22, the config returns a `server` block (dev-server-only in Vite; production/`preview` are unaffected) that binds port 3000 and, at lines 11-13, sets header `"Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*"`. The same block (lines 14-21) proxies /admin, /api, /accounts, /backend, /ajax, /static to the Django backend at http://127.0.0.1:8000. So the finding's factual claims are all accurate: wildcard CORS on the dev server only, proxying to the local backend, no impact on the nginx-served production build. Exploitability is genuinely limited: ACAO:* does not permit reading of credentialed (cookie-authenticated) responses — a cross-origin `fetch` with `credentials:'include'` is blocked when the header is `*` rather than an explicit origin, and a malicious site cannot cause the developer's backend session cookie to be sent otherwise, so only unauthenticated/public proxied responses are actually readable cross-origin. That nuance makes this borderline low/info rather than anything higher, and the claimed severity of low is appropriate and not over-claimed. The proposed fix (remove the wildcard header, or scope to explicit localhost origins if a dev scenario needs it) is directly supported by the cited lines.
verdict.corrected_fix: Delete the `headers` block (lines 11-13) so `server` contains only `port` and `proxy`; the SPA-to-proxy same-origin flow needs no CORS header. If a specific cross-origin dev tool requires it, replace `"*"` with an explicit allowlist of localhost origins. Note that the practical exposure is confined to unauthenticated proxied responses, since `*` cannot expose cookie-authenticated backend data.

security.title: requests lower bound (>=2.26.0) permits multiple credential-leak CVEs
security.description: base.txt pins `requests>=2.26.0,<3`. Everything from 2.26.0 up to the 2.32.x line is permitted, which includes versions with three known CVEs: CVE-2023-32681 (Proxy-Authorization header leaked to the destination host across an HTTPS->HTTP / cross-origin redirect; affects 2.3.0-2.30.0, fixed 2.31.0); CVE-2024-35195 (once a request to a host is made with verify=False, all later requests to that host in the same Session silently skip TLS verification; fixed 2.32.0); CVE-2024-47081 (.netrc credentials can be exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled host via a crafted URL; fixed 2.32.4). setup.py:19 lists `requests` with no version at all. INFERENCE: there is no Python lockfile and CI installs latest-in-range, so a fresh build likely gets a patched 2.32.x; the floor is what is unsafe, not necessarily the running version.
security.impact: For a tool handling clinical/human-subject data that makes outbound HTTP calls, the permitted floor allows silent TLS-verification bypass and leakage of proxy/.netrc credentials to third parties on redirect. Exploitable only if a vulnerable version is actually resolved (e.g. pip cache, internal mirror, or an external --constraint pinning an older release).
security.fix: Raise the floor to the patched release: `requests>=2.32.4,<3` in base.txt, and add the same specifier in setup.py install_requires. Then introduce a lockfile (see separate finding) so the resolved version is guaranteed.

verdict.reason: Verified base.txt:6 = `requests>=2.26.0,<3` and setup.py:19 = bare `requests` in install_requires. No lockfile exists (requirements/ holds only base.txt, dev.txt, docs.txt, ontologies.txt; no *.lock/Pipfile/poetry.lock/constraints), so resolution is unpinned — the finding's premise is accurate. The three CVEs and their fix versions are correct, and the 2.26.0 floor sits below all three fix lines (2.31.0 / 2.32.0 / 2.32.4), so the specifier genuinely permits vulnerable releases. However, the installed version in .venv is requests-2.34.2 (fully patched), which confirms the finding's own caveat that the floor — not the running version — is the issue. Exploitation requires an atypical resolution path (stale pip cache, pinned internal mirror, external --constraint), and default latest-in-range resolution yields a patched build. This is a legitimate but low-severity dependency-hygiene issue, not a live exploitable vuln; the claimed medium overstates real risk. Proposed fix is sound.
verdict.corrected_fix: Raise the floor in both places: `requests>=2.32.4,<3` in requirements/base.txt:6 and add the same specifier for `requests` in setup.py install_requires. Because setup.py currently has no version constraint at all, pinning it there is the higher-value change. Pair with a generated lockfile (pip-compile/uv) so the resolved version is deterministic across environments.

security.title: Django lower bound (>=3.2.23) permits an end-of-life, unpatched release series
security.description: base.txt pins `django>=3.2.23,<6`. Django 3.2 reached end of extended support in April 2024, so the entire 3.2 floor receives no further security patches. 3.2.23 specifically predates the last two 3.2 releases and is missing their fixes: CVE-2024-24680 (denial of service in the `intcomma` handling / date parsing, fixed in 3.2.24) and CVE-2024-27351 (regular-expression denial of service in `django.utils.text.Truncator.words()`, fixed in 3.2.25). setup.py:14 lists `django` with no bound whatsoever. INFERENCE: with no lockfile, a fresh install resolves to the newest release under 6.0 (a supported 5.x at the 2026 cutoff), so the running version is probably fine; the danger is that the floor lets a build land on an EOL, unsupported series with no guardrail failing.
security.impact: Nothing prevents a deployment (pip cache, offline mirror, transitive constraint) from resolving to an EOL Django with unpatched DoS vulnerabilities and no security support. For a clinical data application the framework should never be allowed to float down to an unsupported series.
security.fix: Raise the floor to a currently supported LTS, e.g. `Django>=4.2.16,<6` (or `>=5.2,<6`), and mirror the bound in setup.py. Combine with a lockfile so the exact supported version is pinned.

verdict.reason: All cited facts verified against source. base.txt:1 reads verbatim `django>=3.2.23,<6`; setup.py:14 reads `"django"` with no version bound. No lockfile exists anywhere in the repo (checked requirements/ and root — only base/dev/docs/ontologies .txt, none exact-pinned), so the >=3.2.23 floor is the only guardrail. The CVE mapping is accurate: CVE-2024-24680 (intcomma DoS) fixed in 3.2.24 and CVE-2024-27351 (ReDoS in Truncator.words()) fixed in 3.2.25, and Django 3.2 did reach end of extended support in April 2024, so 3.2.23 is EOL/unpatched. The floor therefore does technically permit installing an unsupported series. However, the impact is speculative: the finding itself concedes default resolution picks the newest allowed release, and I confirmed the .venv actually has Django 5.2.16 (a supported, patched LTS) installed. So the deployed application is not vulnerable; this is a dependency-hygiene/hardening gap, not an active vuln, and the only relevant CVEs are DoS/ReDoS that don't apply to the running version. Medium is over-claimed for a hypothetical resolution scenario — downgraded to low.
verdict.corrected_fix: Raise the floor to a supported LTS and mirror it in setup.py: base.txt -> `Django>=4.2.16,<6` (or `>=5.2,<6`), and setup.py install_requires -> `"django>=4.2.16,<6"`. Add a lockfile (pip-tools compiled requirements or equivalent) so the exact supported version is pinned for reproducible builds. This is a hygiene/defense-in-depth improvement rather than a fix for an active vulnerability, since the resolved version (5.2.16) is already supported.

security.title: djangorestframework lower bound (>=3.12.4) permits browsable-API XSS (CVE-2024-21520)
security.description: base.txt pins `djangorestframework>=3.12.4,<4`. Versions below 3.15.2 are affected by CVE-2024-21520, a reflected cross-site-scripting flaw in the Browsable API (unescaped rendering via the `break_long_headers` template filter). The floor 3.12.4 is well inside the vulnerable range, and setup.py:15 lists `djangorestframework` unversioned. INFERENCE: a fresh install resolves to a patched 3.15.x/3.16.x; the floor is the exposure. Impact is contingent on the Browsable API renderer being enabled in production.
security.impact: If a vulnerable DRF is resolved and the Browsable API is reachable, an attacker can reflect script into a researcher/clinician's authenticated session (session/token theft, actions in the victim's context). Mitigated in practice if the Browsable renderer is disabled in prod, but the floor should not permit the vulnerable code at all.
security.fix: Set `djangorestframework>=3.15.2,<4` in base.txt and add the same bound in setup.py; confirm the Browsable API renderer is disabled in production settings as defense in depth.

verdict.reason: Both cited locations verified. base.txt:2 contains exactly `djangorestframework>=3.12.4,<4`; the floor 3.12.4 with upper bound <4 does permit the full sub-3.15.2 range affected by CVE-2024-21520 (reflected XSS in DRF's Browsable API via the break_long_headers filter, patched in 3.15.2). setup.py:15 lists `djangorestframework` unversioned in install_requires, imposing no floor. security.title: No Python dependency lockfile — backend versions are unpinned/unverifiable and drift
security.description: The backend has only range-based requirements files and no lockfile (no requirements.txt with hashes, no Pipfile.lock, no poetry.lock, no constraints file — confirmed by directory listing). CI runs `pip install -r requirements/dev.txt` (lint_and_test.yml:33) with no pinning, so every build resolves latest-in-range and the exact dependency set is neither reproducible nor auditable. Several packages carry no upper bound or no version at all: `psycopg2-binary` (base.txt:4, fully unpinned), `pandas` (base.txt:7, fully unpinned), `natsort` (base.txt:8), and every line in docs.txt (sphinx, sphinx-django-command, sphinx-rtd-theme, sphinxcontrib-mermaid, myst-parser — all unpinned). setup.py:13-25 lists the entire install_requires with no version specifiers and even includes `numpy`, which is absent from base.txt, so `pip install .` and `pip install -r requirements/base.txt` produce different dependency sets.
security.impact: Builds are non-reproducible; a compromised or yanked upstream release, or a newly disclosed CVE, silently enters production with no pinned baseline to detect or roll back to. Security review cannot state what is actually deployed. Divergence between setup.py and requirements/*.txt means the audited manifest may not match an installed one.
security.fix: Generate and commit a fully pinned, hashed lockfile (pip-tools `pip-compile --generate-hashes`, or uv/Poetry) and have CI install from it with `--require-hashes`. Add upper bounds to psycopg2-binary and pandas, pin the docs deps, and reconcile setup.py install_requires with requirements/base.txt (including numpy). Wire a scheduled `pip-audit`/Dependabot scan against the lockfile.

verdict.reason: All cited locations were opened and every factual claim verified. requirements/ contains only base.txt, dev.txt, docs.txt, ontologies.txt; a find for *.lock, Pipfile*, poetry.lock, constraints*.txt, and any requirements.txt returned nothing — no lockfile and no hashes exist. .github/workflows/lint_and_test.yml:33 runs `pip install -r requirements/dev.txt` with no pinning/--require-hashes. In base.txt, line 4 `psycopg2-binary`, line 7 `pandas`, and line 8 `natsort` are fully unpinned (SQLAlchemy>=2, python-dateutil>=2.8.0, unicodecsv>=0.14.1 have lower but no upper bounds). docs.txt lines 4-8 (sphinx, sphinx-django-command, sphinx-rtd-theme, sphinxcontrib-mermaid, myst-parser) are all bare. setup.py:13-25 install_requires lists all deps with no version specifiers and includes `numpy` (line 24), which is absent from base.txt, so `pip install .` and `pip install -r requirements/base.txt` diverge. The finding is genuine and accurately sourced. Minor caveats: the phrase 'every build resolves latest-in-range' is slightly overstated since django/DRF/crispy-forms/requests do carry upper bounds. Severity: this is a supply-chain/build-reproducibility hardening gap (CWE-1104 class) with no demonstrated active vulnerability, no exposed secret, and no evidence a currently-vulnerable version is being installed; most production deps carry version bounds. Medium is slightly over-claimed for a pure hygiene finding — low is more accurate, though the complete absence of any hash verification and the fully-unpinned production deps keep it a legitimate concern worth fixing.
verdict.corrected_fix: Adopt pip-tools: maintain the human-edited requirements/*.in files and generate pinned, hashed lockfiles via `pip-compile --generate-hashes` (e.g., requirements/base.txt as compiled output), then have CI install with `pip install --require-hashes -r requirements/dev.txt`. Add upper bounds to psycopg2-binary and pandas in the source manifest. Either delete setup.py's redundant/unpinned install_requires or reconcile it with base.txt (add numpy to base.txt or drop it from setup.py) so the audited manifest matches what is installed. security.title: Path traversal / arbitrary file read-write in backup & restore commands
security.description: prepare_backup_file_path builds the target path as `os.path.join(backup_dir, filename)` (chiron/helpers.py:149) with no validation that the result stays inside the backup directory. `filename` is taken directly from the CLI positional arg (chiron_restore_dataset.py:52-55, :85) and `backup_dir` from --backup-dir (:61-66). Because os.path.join treats an absolute component as a reset, `manage.py chiron_restore_dataset /etc/anything.json` reads that absolute path (opened and json.load'd at restore_dataset.py:92-93), and `../` segments in a relative filename escape CHIRON_DATA_DICT_BACKUP_DIR (default 'chiron_config/backups'). The backup command's `open(filepath, 'w')` (chiron_backup_dataset.py:163) will likewise write JSON to a traversed/absolute path.
security.impact: An operator (or a script/cron invoking these commands with attacker-influenced arguments) can read or overwrite files outside the intended backup directory. Exploitation requires the ability to run manage.py, so this is a hardening gap rather than a remote vulnerability - these are CLI management commands, not HTTP endpoints. Impact is limited to environments where command arguments are derived from untrusted input.
security.fix: In prepare_backup_file_path, reject absolute filenames and normalize+contain the path: `base = Path(backup_dir).resolve(); target = (base / filename).resolve(); if not target.is_relative_to(base): raise ValueError('filename escapes backup dir')`. At minimum call os.path.basename(filename) before joining so directory components are stripped.

verdict.reason: Every element of the finding checks out against the source. helpers.py:149 is exactly `filepath = os.path.join(backup_dir, filename)` inside prepare_backup_file_path (lines 133-151), with no normalization or containment check — the only path work is `Path(backup_dir).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` on the directory, and `os.path.exists`. `os` and `Path` are both imported (helpers.py:7-8). In chiron_restore_dataset.py the `filename` is the CLI positional arg (add_arguments lines 52-55; read at handle() line 85) and `backup_dir` comes from `--backup-dir` (lines 61-66); the returned filepath is passed straight to `open(filepath, "r")` and `json.load(f)` at lines 92-93. In chiron_backup_dataset.py the same helper is called at line 72 with `--filename`/`--backup-dir` operator-controlled values and the result is written via `open(filepath, "w")` + `json.dump` at lines 163-164. os.path.join's documented behavior — an absolute second component discards the first, and `../` segments in a relative filename are not collapsed away — means `chiron_restore_dataset /etc/foo.json` reads an absolute path and `../` escapes CHIRON_DATA_DICT_BACKUP_DIR (default confirmed as 'chiron_config/backups' at chiron_settings.py:191). So arbitrary-path read (restore) and arbitrary-path JSON write/overwrite (backup) are both genuinely reachable. Severity 'low' is correctly calibrated and not over-claimed: these are Django manage.py management commands, not HTTP endpoints, so exploitation presupposes the ability to run manage.py — a caller who already has that generally has direct filesystem access. It is a real hardening gap (relevant only where command args derive from untrusted input, e.g. a wrapper script/cron), exactly as the finding itself states. One minor accuracy caveat on the read side: json.load will raise on any non-JSON target, so the arbitrary-read primitive is practically limited to JSON-parseable files (or whatever a decode-error message might echo); the arbitrary-write on the backup path is the cleaner impact.
verdict.corrected_fix: The proposed fix is sound. Prefer the containment check over bare basename so a legitimately nested backup layout still works: `base = Path(backup_dir).resolve(); target = (base / filename).resolve(); if not target.is_relative_to(base): raise ValueError('filename escapes backup dir')` (is_relative_to is fine — the venv is Python 3.12). Apply the same validation to both the restore and backup call sites (it lives in the shared helper, so one fix covers both). If broader compatibility is ever needed, `os.path.commonpath([base, target]) == base` is an equivalent pre-3.9 form.

security.title: Upstream error-response bodies (Django DEBUG tracebacks) are captured verbatim into unprotected on-disk artifacts

efficiency.title: CSV export buffers the entire dataset in memory (no streaming, no row cap)
efficiency.description: generate_cohort_csv() calls querytool.get_full_report(output_type="csv") (export.py:91), which runs the unbounded SQL statement (querytool.py:92 get_sql_statement() with no skip/limit) and materializes EVERY row into a Python list in QueryToolPostgres.run(): `response = []; for row in conn.execute(statement): response.append(list(row))` (querytool.py:33-35). That full list is then post-processed by get_display_values() and written row-by-row into a plain django.http.HttpResponse (export.py:101 `HttpResponse(content_type="text/csv")`, writer loop 103-106). HttpResponse buffers the whole body before sending, so at peak the process holds the full result set as a Python list AND the fully-rendered CSV bytes simultaneously (~2x the data). There is no LIMIT and no configurable cap; export_csv (report_tools.py:132-151, query_tools.py:72-95) exposes this on GET with only a cohort/table def. For a clinical dataset a report can be hundreds of thousands to millions of rows.
efficiency.impact: Large exports spike memory and can OOM/kill the worker; the client also waits for the entire CSV to be built before the first byte is sent (no time-to-first-byte, long-held worker, higher timeout risk). Concurrent large exports multiply the effect.
efficiency.fix: Return a StreamingHttpResponse driven by a generator instead of HttpResponse. Use a server-side/streaming cursor (SQLAlchemy `conn.execution_options(stream_results=True)` / `yield_per`) so rows are pulled in batches rather than fully buffered, and yield each CSV line via csv.writer writing to an Echo/pseudo-buffer. This keeps memory ~O(batch) instead of O(rows) and starts streaming immediately. Expected benefit: memory for a 1M-row export drops from GB-scale to a few MB, and TTFB drops from tens of seconds to sub-second.

efficiency.title: Cohort/stats cache keys include random entry_ids and are order-sensitive, crushing hit rate
efficiency.description: cohort_def_hash is md5(to_json_string(cohort_def)) with no normalization (also duplicated in chiron/cache/cached_cohort.py:37-41). Each cohort_def entry carries an entry_id produced by helpers.generate_entry_id (chiron/helpers.py:41-49), a random 12-char string, so two logically identical cohorts built independently serialize to different JSON and never share a cache entry; reordering entries also changes the hash. The code's own TODOs at hashing.py:7 and cached_cohort.py:38 flag this. This directly limits reuse of CachedCohort (subject counts) and CachedConceptStats.
efficiency.impact: With caches enabled, cohort-count and concept-stat cache hit rates are far lower than they should be - shared/saved cohorts and repeat sessions re-run full research-DB queries that a normalized key would have served from cache.
efficiency.fix: Canonicalize cohort_def before hashing: strip or normalize entry_ids, sort entries and object keys deterministically, then hash. Apply the same normalization in cached_cohort.py and cached_concept_stats.py so both caches key on cohort semantics, not incidental JSON.

verdict.reason: Read all cited locations and confirmed every mechanical claim. hashing.py:6-10: create_cohort_def_hash = md5(to_json_string(cohort_def)) with zero normalization, and line 7 carries the exact TODO 'try to give same hash for irrelevant changes like different order or entry_ids'. cached_cohort.py:37-41 duplicates this logic verbatim with the same TODO (line 38). helpers.py:41-49: generate_entry_id() returns a random 12-char alphanumeric string. Verified entry_id is a real per-entry field of cohort_def entries and is set from this random generator (cohort_def_processor.py:311 response['entry_id'] = helpers.generate_entry_id(); referenced pervasively as criteria_set['entry_id'] in query_definition/cohort_def_functions.py), so the random ids are inside the JSON that gets hashed. to_json_string/make_json_encodable preserve list and dict insertion order, so both reordering entries and differing random entry_ids change the serialized string and hence the md5. Both CachedCohortWrapper.find_matching_cache_entry (cached_cohort.py:49-53) and CachedConceptStatsWrapper.find_matching_cache_entry (cached_concept_stats.py:46-52) filter on cohort_def_hash, so both caches are affected. This is purely a cache hit-rate/efficiency defect (no correctness impact) and is acknowledged by the code's own TODOs. One nuance: the impact is slightly over-broad. A genuinely persisted/shared cohort reloaded from its stored cohort_def keeps its persisted entry_ids and order, so that path would still hit the cache; the real losses are cross-user sharing of independently-constructed logically-identical cohorts (the use case the paired subject_permission_hash exists to enable) and any rebuild/reorder of an equivalent definition. Medium is a defensible severity given each miss triggers a full research-DB query and the defect defeats the intended cross-user/cross-build cache reuse.
verdict.corrected_fix: Introduce one shared canonicalization helper and use it in all three call sites (hashing.create_cohort_def_hash, cached_cohort.set_cohort_def_hash, cached_concept_stats via hashing): deep-copy cohort_def, recursively strip or blank entry_id (and any relative-date target_entry_id references, remapping them consistently so referential semantics are preserved), sort entries deterministically, and serialize with json.dumps(sort_keys=True) before md5. Preserving relative-date references matters because entry_id is used as a link target (target_entry_id) in event/date rules, so naive stripping could conflate semantically different cohorts; normalize those references rather than dropping them. Add a unit test asserting two independently-built logically-identical cohorts produce the same hash and that reordering does not change it.

efficiency.title: create_indexes() builds a plain btree for EVERY published concept, including unbounded Text columns, in one non-concurrent transaction
efficiency.description: create_indexes() loops over every published concept in the dataset (db_writer.py:426-429) and unconditionally issues `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_<concept> ... (<concept>)` as a default btree (db_writer.py:447-453), plus one per subfield for complex types (455-467). Three concerns: (1) It indexes ALL concept columns, including free-text/notes and display-only fields that are never used in a WHERE/JOIN, causing large index bloat and slower ETL finalize for wide datasets (thousands of concepts -> thousands of indexes). (2) A btree over an unbounded Text column fails when a value exceeds Postgres's 2704-byte btree limit; here the failure path prints a warning and calls sys.exit(1) (db_writer.py:472-477), aborting the whole ETL. (3) All CREATE INDEX statements run in a single transaction committed only at the very end (db_writer.py:479-480) and are non-CONCURRENT; any mid-loop failure rolls back every index. Filter columns (in_/=) do benefit from these btrees (see cohort_def/text.py:326 column.in_()), so the btrees are useful for equality/range filtering — the problem is indexing indiscriminately and the text/size failure mode.
efficiency.impact: On wide datasets the index set inflates storage and lengthens ETL; a single long free-text concept can abort the entire index build (and thus the ETL) via sys.exit(1). Non-concurrent single-transaction builds hold locks and consume memory proportional to concept count.

For text/ontology concepts use gin_trgm_ops (or an expression index on left(col,N)) instead of a raw btree so long values don't error. Commit periodically rather than one giant transaction, and consider CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY for non-staging rebuilds. Expected benefit: smaller index footprint, faster ETL, and elimination of the long-text abort path.

Because a headline claim is demonstrably wrong and the true residual issues affect only a clearable cache table (query still works via bitmap index intersection; .first() returns a valid entry; worst case is table bloat, not incorrect results), the claimed medium severity is over-stated. efficiency.title: Only caching layer for concept stats / cohort counts is off by default, with no short-TTL fallback on hot paths
efficiency.description: CHIRON_USE_CACHES defaults False (line 246). efficiency.title: Cache wrappers eagerly compute hashes (incl. a DB query) even when caching is disabled, twice on the cohort-count path
efficiency.description: CachedConceptStatsWrapper.__init__ calls set_subject_permission_hash (line 23) and set_cohort_def_hash (line 24) unconditionally; set_subject_permission_hash -> hashing.create_subject_permission_hash -> chironuser.list_concepts_for_allowed_subjects() which runs PermissionGroup.dataset_uses_permission_groups (a query, data_definition_models.py:727-735) plus permission_groups.all(), and set_cohort_def_hash serializes the whole cohort_def to JSON + md5. The CHIRON_USE_CACHES check happens only later inside find_matching_cache_entry/save (lines 44, 56), so all of this runs and is discarded when caches are off. get_statistics constructs this wrapper on every call (cohort_def_processor.py:81). CachedCohortWrapper has the same pattern (cached_cohort.py:15-19), and QueryToolPostgres.get_cohort_count constructs it TWICE per count - once for read (querytool.py:114) and again for the write attempt (querytool.py:128) - doubling the wasted hashing/DB work when caches are disabled.

efficiency.fix: Early-return on CHIRON_USE_CACHES at the top of the wrapper constructors (or before constructing them in get_statistics/get_cohort_count), and/or compute the hashes lazily on first use. Reuse a single wrapper instance across the read/write branches in get_cohort_count instead of building two.

verdict.reason: Every link in the claim verified against source. cached_concept_stats.py:15-24: __init__ unconditionally calls set_subject_permission_hash() (line 23) and set_cohort_def_hash() (line 24); the CHIRON_USE_CACHES guard exists only inside find_matching_cache_entry (line 44) and save_new_cache_entry (line 56), so the hashing always runs even when caches are off. set_subject_permission_hash -> hashing.create_subject_permission_hash (hashing.py:18) -> chironuser.list_concepts_for_allowed_subjects(); for a real ChironUser (user_models.py:148) this executes PermissionGroup.dataset_uses_permission_groups -> PermissionGroup.objects.filter(dataset=dataset) (a DB query, data_definition_models.py:733), plus self.permission_groups.all() (line 162) when permission groups are in use. set_cohort_def_hash does to_json_string + md5. chiron_settings.py:246 confirms CHIRON_USE_CACHES defaults to False, so caches-off is the default and all this work is discarded. get_statistics (cohort_def_processor.py:81) builds the wrapper on every call before the cache check. efficiency.fix: Define TimeStampedModel once in a new chiron/models/base.py (or abstract_models.py) and `from .base import TimeStampedModel` in the four model files. Remove the three duplicate class bodies.

efficiency.fix: Delete the file, or if intentionally kept as a dev utility, move it out of management/commands (it cannot run there anyway) and correct the help string to describe the destructive delete.

efficiency.title: No response compression (GZip) configured for large JSON/CSV payloads

rejected.title: Latent SQL-text injection via raw string passed to SQLAlchemy order_by()

Currently the only caller path (get_subdocuments -> get_subjects_with_subcollection_data at _source_self_funcs.py:65-67) never passes the argument, so it defaults to None and the branch is dead. Unlike the rest of the query engine — which resolves order targets to SQLAlchemy Column objects (order_by_builder.py:11-13, query_builder.py) — this one uses the raw string.

rejected.fix: Resolve the sort target to a real column object before ordering, e.g. `subcol_stmt = subcol_stmt.order_by(getattr(table.c, sort_concept_id))`, which both validates the identifier against actual columns and lets SQLAlchemy quote it. Avoid passing bare strings to order_by().

BUT the finding's core security premise is false for this project. requirements/base.txt pins `SQLAlchemy>=2` (installed 2.0.27), and the claim that "modern SQLAlchemy coerces a bare string into a textual SQL fragment (a ColumnClause treated as literal SQL)" is the pre-1.4 behavior that was deliberately removed. I verified empirically on the installed SQLAlchemy 2.0.27: passing a string to `order_by()` is treated as a label reference, not literal SQL. A string that matches a column label resolves to that Column (SELECT ... ORDER BY mytable.age); ANY other string — including an injection payload like "age; DROP TABLE mytable; --" or a plain unknown identifier — raises `CompileError: Can't resolve label reference for ORDER BY / GROUP BY / DISTINCT etc. Textual SQL expression ... should be explicitly declared as text(...)`. Therefore there is no ORDER BY SQL injection here, present or latent: a hypothetical future caller wiring user input into sort_concept_id would get a hard CompileError for anything not matching an exact column label, not silent SQL injection. Literal SQL injection would require an explicit, deliberate text() wrapper, which the code does not use. The finding also claims "no compiler warning to stop them," which is the opposite of the actual behavior (a compile-time error). The premise is inverted, so the vulnerability described does not exist.

If a future caller will accept a user-chosen sort field, the correct concern is UX/robustness, not injection: resolving explicitly with `subcol_stmt = subcol_stmt.order_by(getattr(table.c, sort_concept_id))` validates against real columns and raises AttributeError on bad input, which is a reasonable defensive choice — but it should not be framed or prioritized as a SQL-injection fix.

    df = df.astype(str)
